hints: Look at what group each metal is in, because Group 1 and Group 2 metals do not make the same amount of hydrogen per mole.
For 5.0 g, work out moles as 5.0 divided by Ar, and remember calcium gives 1 mole of H2 per mole while potassium gives only 0.5 mole of H2 per mole.
Compare moles of H2 from calcium and potassium first, then check if the heavier metals can catch up despite having fewer moles to start with.
walkthrough:
**Write the two types of reaction with water**

Think of it simply. Group 1 metals make half a hydrogen each, Group 2 metals make a whole hydrogen each.

Group 1 equation:
$$2\text{M} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{MOH} + \text{H}_2$$
Group 2 equation:
$$\text{M} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{M(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$$

**Convert 5.0 g to moles of metal**

Same mass does not mean same moles. Lighter atoms give you more particles to react.

Moles rule:
$$n = \frac{m}{A_r}$$
Using $A_r$: Ca = 40.1, K = 39.1, Rb = 85.5, Sr = 87.6, we get about 0.125 mol Ca, 0.128 mol K, 0.058 mol Rb and 0.057 mol Sr.

**Convert moles of metal to moles of hydrogen**

Now apply the ratio from Step 1. Multiply Group 1 moles by 1/2, keep Group 2 moles as they are.

$$n(\text{H}_2) = 0.5 \times n(\text{M}) \text{ for K and Rb}$$
$$n(\text{H}_2) = 1 \times n(\text{M}) \text{ for Ca and Sr}$$
This gives: Ca about 0.125 mol, K about 0.064 mol, Sr about 0.057 mol, Rb about 0.029 mol.

**Link to gas volume and choose**

Under the same temperature and pressure, volume is directly proportional to moles of gas, so most moles means largest volume.

$$V \propto n$$
Calcium gives the most $\text{H}_2$, so calcium gives the largest volume.

options.A: Calcium is correct. It has a low Ar (40.1) so 5.0 g is about 0.125 mol, and as a Group 2 metal it gives 1 mol H2 per mol. That is about 0.125 mol H2, more than any other metal here.
options.B: Potassium is tempting because it is also light (Ar 39.1) and gives slightly more moles of metal than calcium. The trap is forgetting the stoichiometry: 2K gives only 1H2, so its H2 is halved to about 0.064 mol, only half that of calcium.
options.C: Rubidium is incorrect. It is Group 1 so it only gives 0.5 mol H2 per mol, and it is also heavy (Ar 85.5) so 5.0 g is very few moles. It gives the smallest amount of H2, about 0.029 mol.
options.D: Strontium is incorrect. Although it is Group 2 and gives 1 mol H2 per mol like calcium, it is much heavier (Ar 87.6). So 5.0 g is only about 0.057 mol, giving less than half the hydrogen of calcium.
